prompts.promptVerbatim: Describe the specific chromosomal abnormality responsible for Down syndrome.
prompts.supported: Down syndrome is trisomy 21. Nondisjunction is failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate; the deck also describes Robertsonian translocation involving fused long arms. Keep a chromosome-number change distinct from a structural rearrangement.

The packet associates cognitive impairment with Down syndrome, cri du chat, fragile X, untreated PKU, Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. PKU illustrates why genotype does not alone determine phenotype: treatment changes the expressed outcome without removing the genotype.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Complete etiologic classification, mechanisms and diagnostic distinctions beyond these selected examples.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What gene abnormality causes cystic fibrosis
prompts.supported: The supplied mechanism is defective chloride-channel transport, salt imbalance, and thick dehydrated mucus affecting lungs and pancreas. It is an autosomal recessive example. The slide's absolute survival statement is excluded as a dated claim.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: The requested named gene and precise mutation details are not supplied; obtain the ninth-edition CF passage.

prompts.promptVerbatim: How is a recessive disease inherited
prompts.supported: A recessive disease requires two abnormal alleles in the supplied autosomal model. Two heterozygous carriers have, for each pregnancy, 25% affected offspring, 50% carriers and 25% unaffected noncarriers. Both sexes can be affected.

The chapter objective names hemophilia, and the deck teaches general X-linked recessive rules. It does not explicitly connect Hemophilia A to a pattern or provide its molecular defect. General inheritance teaching appears below; the Hemophilia-specific key is gated.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Hemophilia A inheritance, factor defect and recurrence examples from the assigned textbook.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Risk factors for DM II; why is obesity an important risk factor in DM II?
prompts.supported: Risk factors include obesity and family history. Obesity increases insulin resistance: cells have difficulty using the insulin present. Production can also diminish. Exercise has a preventive effect in the supplied deck. Do not substitute the autoimmune beta-cell destruction described for type 1 diabetes.

Carcinoma means a malignant epithelial tumor; adenocarcinoma specifies ducts or glands. Sarcoma identifies malignant connective tissue, lymphoma lymphatic tissue, and leukemia blood-forming cells. Benign growth is well differentiated, noninvasive and nonmetastatic in the supplied contrast.

prompts.promptVerbatim: How do cancer cells gain access to the circulation?
prompts.supported: Invasion precedes metastasis. Cancer cells secrete proteases that digest extracellular matrix and basement membranes, opening pathways for movement. Cells must then survive travel through blood or lymph and grow in a receptive distant environment. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition reduces adhesion and increases migration and resistance to apoptosis.

Adjuvant chemotherapy follows surgical excision to eliminate micrometastases. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy precedes local surgery or radiation. Induction chemotherapy aims at shrinkage or disappearance of tumors. Timing and purpose are different classification axes.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Most common time childhood cancers are diagnosed
prompts.supported: Childhood cancers are often diagnosed during peak physical growth. The notes specify that embryonal tumors begin during intrauterine life and are typically diagnosed by age five. This latter age statement describes embryonal tumors, not every childhood cancer.
Both decks identify prenatal DES exposure among exposures associated with childhood cancer susceptibility. Exposure is a risk association, not proof that an individual child will develop cancer.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Specific DES-related tumor, exposed population, mechanism and latency are absent.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Where do most childhood cancers arise from?
prompts.supported: Most childhood cancers arise from the mesodermal germ layer, which produces connective tissue, bone, cartilage, muscle, blood, vessels, gonads, kidneys and lymphatic tissue. Embryonal tumors reflect immature tissue that fails to mature or differentiate.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Pediatric cancers and the N-myc oncogene
prompts.supported: The speaker notes explicitly associate N-myc with neuroblastoma. The same notes distinguish Down syndrome and leukemia, tuberous sclerosis and glial tumors, and Gorlin syndrome and medulloblastoma.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Amplification mechanism, prognostic meaning and treatment implications are not supplied.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Gland responsible for thermoregulation and cooling
prompts.supported: Eccrine sweat glands cool the body through evaporation. Sebaceous glands secrete sebum. The dermis contains vessels, nerves, follicles and glands; fibroblasts make connective matrix and collagen, while mast cells release histamine. Subcutaneous tissue contains adipocytes and connective tissue.

Unrelieved pressure occludes capillary flow and causes ischemia and necrosis. Stage I has nonblanchable redness with intact skin; stage II partial skin loss; stage III full skin loss reaching subcutaneous tissue; stage IV damage to muscle, bone or supporting structures. A slough-covered base is unstageable; deep red or purple intact skin can signal deep tissue injury. Repositioning, pressure relief and moisture control address contributing forces.

Excess collagen and abnormal fibroblast activity create a keloid. It is elevated, firm and progressively extends beyond the original injury. A hypertrophic scar remains inside the injury border. The boundary is the useful discriminator, rather than elevation alone.

Psoriasis is a relapsing T-cell-mediated proliferative disorder. Epidermal turnover shortens from 26–30 to 3–4 days, leaving inadequate time for maturation. Plaque is most common; inverse is rare; guttate is more common in children; pustular develops pus; erythrodermic produces widespread red scaling. Arthritis and nail disease are listed systemic complications. Treatment ranges from emollients and topical agents to phototherapy and systemic agents according to severity.

Varicella-zoster virus causes both chickenpox and shingles. Chickenpox shows lesions at different stages together and spreads through contact or airborne droplets. Reactivation produces vesicles along a sensory nerve distribution. Do not confuse initial widespread infection with the later dermatomal eruption.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Scleroderma definition, patho and clinical manifestations
prompts.supported: The slide describes sclerosis, fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis associated with T-helper cells and cytokines. Skin is hard, hypopigmented, taut and shiny. Its heading says localized morphea but its text also mentions internal-organ progression; this subtype boundary needs clarification before scoring.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Clarify localized versus systemic scleroderma and the full manifestations and pathophysiology in the ninth edition. No subtype-progression key is used.

prompts.supported: Cold injury involves inflammation and reperfusion. Frostbite freezes tissue with ice-crystal formation, progressing from distal to proximal areas. Skin may be white or yellowish, waxy and firm.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Named inflammatory mediators and their roles in frostbite are absent.

prompts.supported: The frostbite treatment slide lists analgesics but does not identify ibuprofen or its mechanism. Ibuprofen appears elsewhere for burn metabolism; that does not establish a frostbite-specific claim.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Assigned textbook passage linking ibuprofen to frostbite inflammatory mediators, purpose and regimen.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Atopic dermatitis: which Ig, clinical manifestations, patho, lab results
prompts.supported: Two explanatory models connect immune dysregulation and epidermal barrier failure. Filaggrin alteration weakens the barrier. Severe itching is the hallmark; redness, edema, scaling and scratching-related lichenification occur. Infants commonly have face, scalp, trunk and extensor lesions, while older children favor flexures. Hydration, emollients and trigger avoidance support barrier care.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Requested immunoglobulin and laboratory findings are absent; obtain exact Ig/lab passage.

prompts.supported: Prolonged urine/feces exposure, wet friction and occlusion irritate skin. Secondary Candida infection produces strongly erythematous, sharply bounded lesions with pustulovesicular satellites. Frequent changes, air exposure and barrier protection reduce irritation; candidal involvement adds a topical antifungal in the supplied treatment.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Impetigo, Tinea, Thrush: patho, clinical manifestations, source of infection and definition
prompts.supported: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection transmitted by direct or indirect contact. Nonbullous lesions form honey-colored crusts; bullous disease involves staphylococcal exfoliative toxin disrupting adhesion. Dermatophytes thrive on keratin; their infections are called tinea. Capitis affects scalp and breaks hair; corporis expands outward with central clearing, often following kitten or puppy contact. Candida causes oral thrush with white plaques and shallow ulcers. The deck lists KOH examination for tinea and antifungal treatment for tinea and thrush.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Goals in treatment of shock in children
prompts.supported: Restore oxygen delivery and tissue perfusion while treating the cause. Volume support addresses hypovolemia; myocardial support addresses cardiogenic shock; eliminating obstruction addresses obstructive shock. Airway, oxygenation and ventilation remain central. Normal systolic pressure alone does not establish adequate perfusion.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know all types of shock in adults and children-pathophysiology, clinical manifestations and management
prompts.teachingTitle: Shock types: mechanism, findings and management
prompts.supported: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure despite available volume; hypovolemic shock is inadequate circulating volume; neurogenic shock loses vascular tone; anaphylaxis creates vasodilation and fluid shift after an allergen; sepsis causes inflammatory maldistribution; obstruction physically impedes blood flow. Adult neurogenic findings include bradycardia and low vascular resistance. Pediatric compensated shock retains age-appropriate systolic pressure despite poor perfusion. The detailed comparison card separates treatment goals and supplied findings.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Exhaustive adult obstructive shock and pediatric anaphylaxis management, complete dosing/sequencing, and current protocol clarification are absent. Neurogenic adult treatment is only briefly listed. Pediatric lactate units and sepsis table wording need correction.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Burns all levels in adults and children-pathophysiology, definitions, clinical manifestations, determination of severity, calculation of body surface burned and management, complications
prompts.teachingTitle: Burns: depths, severity, calculation and care
prompts.supported: Burn injury can be thermal, chemical or electrical. Epidermal-only, partial dermal and full-thickness destruction differ in preserved barriers and appendages. Full-thickness injury destroys nerve endings and may be painless; superficial dermal injury is painful and blistering. Age, site, depth and extent determine severity. Children lose more fluid per unit weight because of a larger surface-area-to-weight ratio. Urine output monitors resuscitation. Airway compromise, infection, hypermetabolism, scarring and contracture complicate recovery. Age-adjusted charts are needed for children.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Validated adult rule-of-nines diagram, corrected pediatric percentages, calculation examples, modified Parkland formula, complete depth-specific management and dose protocols are missing. Chapter 49 slide 45 lower-extremity percentage is quarantined. Chapter 48 uses inconsistent first-degree/partial-thickness terminology; teach tissue depth explicitly.

prompts.supported: The supplied marker for the end of burn shock is capillary seal. Distinguish this event from a bedside measure of adequate fluid resuscitation, for which the deck identifies urine output.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Renal failure in electrical burns in children
prompts.supported: The packet names electrical burns and describes renal changes after burns generally, but supplies no electrical-burn-specific renal failure mechanism.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Electrical injury, muscle breakdown/pigment injury and renal failure passage from the assigned textbook; no inferred key.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Characteristics of Klinefelter syndrome, Turner syndrome, Cri du chat syndrome
prompts.supported: Turner syndrome is 45,X with short stature, neck webbing, widely spaced nipples and ovarian absence in the deck. Klinefelter includes at least one Y and two X chromosomes, small testes, sparse body hair and gynecomastia. Cri du chat is a deletion syndrome with low birth weight, microcephaly and cognitive impairment.

Mycosis means fungal disease; tinea specifically denotes dermatophyte disease. Site labels matter: capitis scalp, pedis foot, corporis body, cruris groin and unguium nail. Candida can shift from commensal organism to pathogen in warm moist conditions and in listed host-risk states. KOH scrapings can reveal fungal hyphae.

The subcutaneous layer contains adipocytes and connective tissue, with collagen continuous with dermal collagen. Keep this layer distinct from the outer epidermis and the gland-, vessel- and nerve-containing dermis.

Markers are substances produced by benign or malignant cells, found in/on cells or in fluids such as blood, urine or spinal fluid. Examples include hormones, enzymes, genes and antigens. AFP is associated with liver/germ-cell tumors and PSA with prostate tumors. A marker can support screening, diagnosis or course monitoring without being uniquely cancer-specific.

The packet links inherited APC mutation with familial adenomatous polyposis and discusses preventive colectomy in the high-risk condition. It also distinguishes hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Polyp morphology, histologic categories, clinical manifestations and malignant-potential comparison are not supplied.

prompts.supported: Chronic inflammation can promote proliferation and new-vessel growth as part of a persistent wound-healing response. Tumor-associated macrophages can inhibit cytotoxic immune function and produce growth-promoting cytokines and angiogenic factors. This connects tissue repair signals with tumor survival rather than making every inflammation a cancer diagnosis.

The deck links smoking to cancers of lung, mouth, lips, nasal cavity/sinuses, larynx, pharynx, esophagus, pancreas, kidney, uterus, cervix, colon/rectum, liver and acute leukemia. Secondhand smoke is linked to lung cancer. These are the supplied positive associations; omissions are not proof of no association.

prompts.supported: Dermal mast cells release histamine. Urticaria is presented as type I hypersensitivity: histamine promotes vascular fluid leakage and transient raised wheals. Allergic contact dermatitis is T-cell-mediated delayed type IV disease. Cutaneous vasculitis involves small-vessel immune complexes and complement.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Full reaction-by-layer comparison and detailed mediator sequence beyond the named examples.

prompts.supported: An allergen binds a carrier protein and becomes a sensitizing antigen. Langerhans cells process it and present it to T cells. The delayed type IV response produces erythema, swelling, itching and vesicles. Irritant contact dermatitis is nonimmunologic injury; similar appearance does not establish the same mechanism.
General type I and type IV skin reactions are supplied, but latex and its immunoglobulin relationship are not explicitly taught.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Latex protein allergy versus additive contact sensitivity, relevant immunoglobulin and reaction types from the textbook.

prompts.promptVerbatim: basal cell carcinoma and gene alteration
prompts.supported: The deck associates basal cell carcinoma with TP53 and PTCH1 mutations. The lesion is pearly or ivory with a depressed center and rolled borders. Notes distinguish BRAF/RAS associations in cutaneous melanoma.

MODS involves at least two failing organ systems after severe illness or injury. Primary MODS follows the direct insult; secondary MODS reflects an amplified host response, often after another insult. Primed leukocytes, endothelial damage, permeability changes, blood-flow maldistribution and a net procoagulant state impair organs. Confusion, lung dysfunction and renal/hepatic failure are supplied manifestations. Prevention controls the trigger and avoids second insults; support includes oxygenation, nutrition, volume restoration and organ-specific support.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What is transcription? What is nondisjunction?? What is aneuploidy?? What is polyploidy? What is translocation??
prompts.supported: Transcription synthesizes RNA from DNA. Nondisjunction is failed chromosome/chromatid separation. Aneuploidy changes individual chromosome number; polyploidy adds complete chromosome sets beyond diploidy. Translocation interchanges material between nonhomologous chromosomes. Do not equate a copied RNA message with a chromosome-number error.
Codominance is defined as expression of both alleles, but ABO alleles and blood-group crosses are absent.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: ABO genotype/phenotype table, dominance relationships and worked inheritance crosses.

prompts.supported: The expressivity example, von Recklinghausen disease, is autosomal dominant and ranges from brown skin spots to tumors, scoliosis, gliomas and neuromas. This teaches variation in expression, not a complete disease classification.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Named gene/protein mechanism, disease types or degrees and diagnostic criteria.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What is penetrance? Expressivity? Dominance? Recessiveness?
prompts.supported: Penetrance measures the fraction with a genotype who show its expected phenotype. Expressivity describes variation in the phenotype. Dominance means one allele's effect is visible with another present; recessiveness means that effect is hidden in the heterozygote. A carrier can transmit a disease allele while remaining phenotypically normal.

Incidence counts new cases over a specified period in a population. Prevalence describes the affected fraction at a point in time. Relative risk divides incidence in an exposed group by incidence in an unexposed group. A snapshot of existing disease cannot substitute for the rate of new cases.

prompts.promptVerbatim: which are cancers that cluster in families?
prompts.supported: Breast and colorectal familial patterns are directly described. Earlier onset and bilateral breast disease strengthen the supplied familial signal. APC mutation is linked with familial adenomatous polyposis. Prostate cancer risk-associated genetic variation is listed without the same recurrence detail.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Exhaustive familial cancer list and syndrome-specific inheritance beyond the supplied examples.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know the BRAC1 and BRAC2 mutations
prompts.supported: The guide's BRAC spelling is rendered BRCA in teaching, following the decks. BRCA1 maps to chromosome 17 and BRCA2 to chromosome 13. The inherited form increases breast and ovarian cancer risk, and the packet discusses preventive surgery for high-risk mutation carriers.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Specific mutation types, molecular DNA-repair mechanism and individualized risk interpretation are not supplied.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Describe the following patterns of inheritance and identify at least two pathological conditions associated with each pattern: a) autosomal recessive b) autosomal dominant c) sex-linked recessive d) sex-linked dominant
prompts.supported: Autosomal dominant inheritance can pass through successive generations in either sex. Autosomal recessive disease appears when both alleles are abnormal. X-linked recessive transmission has no father-to-son route because fathers supply sons with a Y. The packet gives Huntington/von Recklinghausen examples, cystic fibrosis and Duchenne muscular dystrophy; it names X-linked dominant inheritance without teaching it in depth.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Two explicitly supported pathological examples for each requested pattern, especially X-linked dominant and the second recessive examples; complete X-linked dominant rules.
